section_summary: This section is dominated by Japanese-language campaign literature for the April 1946 general election, including Tokyo candidate speeches, Socialist Party newspapers, manifestos, slogans, candidate lists, and policy outlines. Recurring subjects include democratization, socialism versus capitalism, food shortages, inflation, land reform, labor organization, housing, women’s political rights, the emperor system, and postwar reconstruction. The section closes with a confidential U.S. Political Adviser despatch reporting on the final days of the election campaign, minor parties, candidate totals, and possible post-election coalitions.

subfiles.title: Campaign Speeches by Candidates of the First Constituency, Tokyo: Japanese Texts
subfiles.about: Campaign statements present rival candidates’ programs for Japan’s political, economic, and social reconstruction before the 1946 general election.
subfiles.summary: The opening text clearly continues from an earlier page and ranges across democratization, food and housing shortages, inflation, industrial recovery, land ownership, local government, education, women’s rights, and social insurance. Several candidates supply autobiographical statements and present themselves as practical agents of a peaceful, democratic Japan. The speeches repeatedly discuss the emperor system, the occupation, and MacArthur’s reforms while appealing for votes in the Tokyo district.

subfiles.title: Contents Note: Campaign Speeches by Candidates of First Constituency, Tokyo
subfiles.about: An English identification sheet lists prominent elected candidates whose speeches are included in the preceding Japanese campaign material.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies the material as campaign speeches by candidates in Tokyo’s First Constituency. It lists Nakajima Moritoshi, Hayashi Ren, Asanuma Inejirō, Suzuki Senpachi, Takeuchi Shigeyo, Yamaguchi Shizue, and Ishida Tenimatsu, together with their party affiliations.

subfiles.title: Japan Socialist Party Election Bulletin and Campaign Newspaper
subfiles.about: A Socialist Party campaign newspaper combines leaders’ speeches, policy slogans, social commentary, candidate rosters, serialized features, and advertisements.
subfiles.summary: Speeches by Asanuma Inejirō, Suzuki Mosaburō, Katayama Tetsu, Kawano Mitsu, and Mizutani Chōzaburō advocate peaceful democratic socialism, nationalization of key industries, labor rights, land reform, price stabilization, and relief for war victims. Articles examine housing, food deliveries, tenant farming, unemployment, returnees, women workers, rural politics, and the growth of labor unions. The issue also contains national candidate and branch lists, explanatory pieces on socialist thought, literary material, and commercial or publishing advertisements.

subfiles.title: DC/R Routing Slip
subfiles.about: A brief internal routing form records action and copy-distribution fields for the accompanying political material.
subfiles.summary: The page bears the heading “DC/R ROUTING SLIP” and fields for origin, number, action, and copies. Little substantive information survives beyond routing marks and numerals.

subfiles.title: General Election Leaflet: An Appeal to the Nation—Socialism or Capitalism?
subfiles.doc_type: Japan Socialist Party election manifesto or policy leaflet
subfiles.from: Japan Socialist Party Election Strategy Department; Suzuki Mosaburō
subfiles.about: The Socialist Party sets out its principal policies for the general election and argues that Japan must choose socialist reconstruction over renewed capitalism.
subfiles.summary: The leaflet opens with election slogans linking household politics, land for cultivators, minimum living standards, and high-wage production to the broader choice between socialism and capitalism. It calls for democratization, socialization of finance and key industries, land and labor reform, confiscation of wartime profits, and emergency action against inflation, food shortages, unemployment, and homelessness. Extended sections distinguish the Socialist Party from the Progressive, Liberal, and Communist parties and discuss the character of democratic and socialist revolution. The main policy text is credited to Suzuki Mosaburō and dated February 3.

subfiles.title: Election Publicity Address: The Old Year Passes and a New Year Begins
subfiles.about: A campaign address presents defeat as the beginning of a revolutionary democratic stage and outlines Socialist proposals for rebuilding Japan.
subfiles.summary: The address urges voters to abandon the old political order and build a new Japan through parliamentary democracy, constitutional reform, and industrial democracy. It supports retention of a constitutionally limited emperor, stronger powers for the Diet, recognized labor and cooperative organizations, and worker participation in management. Further passages address agricultural production, compulsory rice deliveries, food imports, inflation, taxation, wartime profits, public debt, and minimum living standards. Several later pages preserve fragmented or repeated portions of the same text because of difficult page layout and poor OCR.

subfiles.title: Election Bulletin Outline (Reference 1)
subfiles.doc_type: Party campaign outline or draft election bulletin
subfiles.from: Japan Socialist Party Election Strategy Department
subfiles.about: A concise campaign outline defines the election’s significance, the Socialist Party’s political identity, and its immediate reconstruction program.
subfiles.summary: The outline contrasts the coming democratic election with the wartime Diet election conducted under the Tōjō cabinet and military-bureaucratic control. It describes the party as socially democratic, committed to popular sovereignty, international credibility, and restoration of Japan’s independent political life. The closing fragments connect political democracy with socialist economic reform and urgent measures concerning food, distribution, housing, women, and land.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 358: Political Parties in Japan—Developments During the Week Ending April 6, 1946
subfiles.doc_type: Confidential diplomatic despatch with enclosed weekly political report
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The despatch transmits a weekly report on the climax of Japan’s general-election campaign, candidate filings, minor parties, and prospective coalition alignments.
subfiles.summary: The report describes increasing campaign rallies, press efforts to discourage abstention, weak party organization, high campaign expenses, and public bewilderment over 2,782 candidates. It tabulates candidates by the five major parties, minor parties, and independents, then identifies several noteworthy small parties and discussions of a primary-election system. The report also analyzes Hatoyama Ichirō’s suggestion that a Liberal government might seek Progressive and Social Democratic support, along with rumors involving Shidehara Kijūrō and Mitsuchi Chūzō. The enclosed report continues beyond page 149.
